results.content: Notably, some studies found unidirectional causality from tourism to both CO₂ emissions and economic growth—for example, in OECD countries (Gedikli et al., 2022 Dynamic relationship between international tourism, economic growth and environmental pollution in the OECD countries: evidence from panel VAR model. The results demonstrate the existence of bidirectional causality relationships between the variables analysed in pairs, suggesting a significant interdependence between tourism, economic growth (GDP), and CO₂ emissions in the 15 countries studied. Table 11 presents the results of the Granger causality test applied to each region, allowing for the identification of differences in the relationship between tourism, economic growth (GDP), and environmental impact (CO₂ emissions) in Europe, America, and Asia. In the short term, tourism has a positive effect on GDP, but its relationship with CO₂ emissions differs: in Europe, it is associated with a more sustainable model; in America, it drives economic growth without a clear effect on pollution, and in Asia, its impact is not significant on either variable.

results.title: Ecotourism and economic sustainable development of local ...
results.content: # Ecotourism and economic sustainable development of local communities from the lens of technological innovation: the synergistic role of green industry and social capital. Based on provincial panel data from China spanning 2012 to 2022, this study employs the propensity score matching method to effectively address potential endogeneity concerns. A two-way fixed effects model is further applied to systematically examine the impact mechanism of ecotourism on the economic sustainable development of local communities. The empirical results reveal that ecotourism not only directly contributes to enhancing community sustainability but also exerts a significant mediating effect through the stimulation of technological innovation. Further analysis indicates that the development of green industrial systems and the accumulation of social capital can effectively strengthen the positive impact of ecotourism. Notably, this promotive effect varies across regions, with more pronounced outcomes observed in areas characterized by stronger digital infrastructure, more stable ecological environments, and higher levels of human capital.
